Denied
de-NYDE
v.t. (pret. & pp.)
From Latin denegare, to refuse or say no, from de and negare, to deny. Webster 1828: contradicted; refused; disowned. Scripture applies the word to Peter, to the nation, and, most unexpectedly, to a man who fails to provide for his household.

Biblical Definition

The most famous denial in Scripture is recorded without any softening: But he denied before them all, saying, I know not what thou sayest (Matthew 26:70) — before them all, and the Gospel that reports it most bleakly is Mark, which the church has long held was Peter’s own account. Peter later preaches the same charge to the nation, and the wording is careful: ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you (Acts 3:14). He knew what the word cost. Paul then applies it in a place no one expects: if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8). Denial is not only a word spoken under pressure; it can be a duty left undone at home. And to the church at Philadelphia, the risen Christ names the opposite as the whole of their commendation: thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name (Revelation 3:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DENY as to contradict; to gainsay; to declare a statement untrue; to refuse to grant; to disown, to renounce or reject; hence DENIED, contradicted, refused, disowned.

expand to see more

DENY, v.t. — To contradict; to gainsay; to declare a statement or position not to be true.

To refuse to grant; as, we asked for bread, and it was denied us.

To disown; to refuse to acknowledge; to renounce; as, to deny one’s self.

DENIED, pp. — Contradicted; refused; disowned; renounced.

Latin denegare, from de and nego, to say no — the root of negative.

Key Scripture

Matthew 26:70 — "But he denied before them all, saying, I know not what thou sayest."

Acts 3:14 — "But ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you;"

1 Timothy 5:8 — "But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel."

Revelation 3:8 — "I know thy works: behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name."

Modern Corruption

1 Timothy 5:8 calls failure to provide for one’s household a denial of the faith, which is a far stronger claim about domestic duty than most churches are willing to make.

expand to see more

Paul does not say that neglecting one’s household is inconsistent with the faith or falls short of it; he says the man hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel — worse than an unbeliever, because even unbelievers commonly provide for their own. The context is the church’s care of widows, and the principle is that the family bears the first obligation and the church takes up what the family genuinely cannot. Two errors follow from losing this. The first is the pattern in which a man’s ministry activity is treated as compensating for his household’s neglect, which the qualifications for elder in 1 Timothy 3:4-5 explicitly forbid: he that knows not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God? The second is the assumption that institutional welfare replaces familial duty, which this verse denies.

Peter’s denial is preserved in all four Gospels, and it is worth asking why. The apostle whom the church at Rome regarded as its founder is presented, in the Gospel most closely associated with him, cursing and swearing that he never knew Christ. The early church did not suppress this, which is a mark of the honesty of the record; but the deeper reason is doctrinal. Our Lord had told Peter beforehand that Satan had desired to have him, that He had prayed for him, and that when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren (Luke 22:32). The denial did not surprise Christ and did not sever the man. That is perseverance of the saints exactly as the confession states it: not that the saints never fall grievously, but that they are kept, and restored, by the intercession of Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek arneomai (G720), to deny or disown; aparneomai (G533), to deny utterly; epaischunomai (G1870), to be ashamed of; Latin nego, to say no.

expand to see more

Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, to disown; Peter’s denial (Matthew 26:70), the nation’s (Acts 3:14), and the household’s (1 Timothy 5:8).

Greek aparneomai (G533) — to deny utterly; the word Christ used in foretelling the threefold denial (Matthew 26:34).

Greek apistos (G571) — an unbeliever, an infidel; the comparison in 1 Timothy 5:8.

Greek pronoeo (G4306) — to think of beforehand, to provide; the duty whose neglect is called denial.

Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep or guard; hast kept my word (Revelation 3:8), the opposite of denial.

Usage

"He denied before them all (Matthew 26:70) — recorded in all four Gospels, and most bleakly in Peter’s own."

"He hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8) — denial as a duty left undone at home."

"Hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name (Revelation 3:8) — the whole commendation of a church with little strength."
